title: Everyone Deserves A Good Death
summary: Josh and Chuck (with Jerry and Emily referenced) explore hospice care and the concept of a "good death." They trace hospice history from medieval origins and the mid-20th century shift in medicine's treatment of the dying, through Cicely Saunders' St. Christopher's Hospice in London (1967), Florence Wald's first US hospice in Branford, Connecticut, and the 1982 Medicare hospice benefit. They cover Medicare eligibility (terminal illness, six months or less, forgoing curative treatment), the four levels of hospice care paid as a daily rate, volunteer roles, interdisciplinary teams, growth in hospice use, the stigma and late enrollment, evidence that hospice can extend life, the distinction between hospice, palliative care and medically assisted dying, for-profit and private equity concerns, live discharge rules, and the burdens on families. The episode closes with listener mail about the "Gen Z stare."

segments.title: Opening and the concept of a good death
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode on hospice and the idea of a good death, noting that death talk has become taboo in the US again after a late-2000s surge of interest. He lists components people associate with a good death: saying goodbye, control, freedom from pain, environment, and coming to terms with dying.

segments.title: Pre-hospice medicine and the 1960s-70s shift
segments.summary: The hosts describe how hospitals historically abandoned incurable dying patients, how pain medication was restricted by fears of addiction, and how mid-20th century medical optimism made incurability a reminder of medicine's limits. Elisabeth Kübler-Ross's 1969 book and Ernest Becker's 1973 The Denial of Death helped push the movement forward.

segments.title: Cicely Saunders and the founding of hospice
segments.summary: Cicely Saunders, who had a bad back that kept her from nursing, became a social worker, then a physician after starting medical school at 33. She developed pain protocols, including combining morphine with other medications and tailoring care to patients' preferences, and founded St. Christopher's Hospice in London in 1967. It ended visiting hours and addressed total pain. Florence Wald started the first US hospice in Branford, Connecticut, in 1973. Hosts note the non-denominational nature of hospice.

segments.title: Early US hospice, volunteers, and Medicare benefit
segments.summary: Early American hospices were home-based and largely volunteer-run, with clergy and moonlighting doctors involved. Government noticed cost savings, and the 1982 Medicare hospice benefit covered hospice care and allowed professionally staffed services. Hosts note cost savings from avoiding expensive curative treatment.

segments.title: Hospice eligibility and Medicare coverage
segments.summary: Hospice in the US is usually paid by Medicare or Medicaid, at no charge to the patient, while UK hospice relies largely on donations. Eligibility requires two doctors to certify a terminal illness with six months or less to live and no pursuit of curative treatment.

segments.title: Four levels of hospice care
segments.summary: Medicare pays hospices a daily rate by level of care: routine home care, continuous home care during crises, inpatient respite care up to five days to relieve caregivers, and general inpatient care for symptom management. Palliative care is central, and treating conditions unrelated to the terminal illness is allowed.

segments.title: What hospice workers and volunteers do
segments.summary: Hospice provides bathing, housekeeping, medication help, shopping, babysitting, fundraising help, hair styling, music, comedy, and pet care. Volunteers need only to be present and a driver; Medicare law requires at least five percent of patient hours from volunteers. Interdisciplinary teams include nurses, doctors, social workers, bereavement counselors and clergy, addressing total pain including social and psychological pain.

segments.title: Hospice growth, stigma, and late enrollment
segments.summary: Hospice centers grew from about 2,000 in 2001 to about 5,700 today; utilization rose 32 percent from 2013 to 2022. About half of Americans enroll before death, more often those with cancer, women, the more educated, and older people. Stigma and late referrals, including doctors who see hospice as giving up, mean many patients get little time in hospice.

segments.title: Hospice and longevity; a personal story
segments.summary: Studies suggest stopping curative treatment for hospice can sometimes extend life through better monitoring, symptom control, nutrition and sleep. Josh recounts that Yumi's father left hospice alive after being given days to live and lived three more years, crediting Yumi and the hospice doctor.

segments.title: Hospice vs. medically assisted dying and palliative care
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish hospice and palliative care, which neither hastens nor postpones death, from medically assisted dying, which is legal in some places and requires a doctor's sign-off. Hospice workers often oppose assisted dying, though many hospice people support the right to choose. Palliative care can be given alongside curative treatment. A joke about cocaine and liquor in Wald's protocol closes the section.

segments.title: For-profit hospice and private equity concerns
segments.summary: Hosts discuss for-profit hospice. Being for-profit is not inherently bad, but publicly traded chains and private-equity-owned hospices tend to get lower care ratings. A 2024 survey found 25 percent of US hospices are owned by private equity. The flat daily payment creates incentives to cut staff and corners.

segments.title: Visit requirements, overbilling, and live discharge
segments.summary: Hosts say a commonly cited rule of two visits a month for home hospice is a myth; the federal government sets no minimum visit frequency and enforcement is weak. A study reportedly found for-profit hospices bill Medicare about 34 percent more than nonprofits. Live discharge rules require demonstrating decline at recertification, and discharge can happen after emergencies, which is often unfair.

segments.title: Burdens on families and inadequate home hospice pay
segments.summary: Moving patients between facilities is burdensome for families. When a patient is discharged alive, medical equipment, medications and support stop. Medicare pays the lowest rate for routine non-crisis home hospice, so patients who want to die at home without family or money may have no support.

segments.title: Advice: plan ahead and living wills
segments.summary: Hosts advise families to talk about end-of-life wishes early, to create a living will stating a desire for hospice and to stop curative treatment, and to research and read reviews of hospices before they are needed.

segments.title: Shout-out to hospice doctor
segments.summary: Josh gives a shout-out to Yumi's father's hospice doctor, Doctor Pajari, for listening and helping him get out of hospice.

segments.title: Listener mail: the Gen Z stare
segments.summary: Listeners Josie, Sam and Catherine explain the Gen Z stare as a response to being interrupted, not being taken seriously, online communication, and distrust of fake niceness. The hosts discuss it, and Chuck offers a tip of nodding and saying 'interesting'. Josh closes by inviting generational listener mail to the show's email address.
